label: Refrigerant under pressure
summary: Fridges, freezers, air conditioners, dehumidifiers and heat pumps hold refrigerant under pressure in a sealed loop. Cutting a line sprays liquid that freezes skin and eyes, and in a small room a big leak can push out the air. Many newer units use flammable gas (R-600a isobutane or R-290 propane). Older units may hold ozone-depleting gases. Heated refrigerant can break down into toxic gases.
signs: A sealed loop of copper or aluminium tubing joined to a black dome compressor
A rating plate listing the refrigerant, such as R-134a, R-600a, R-290, R-410A, R-22 or R-12
'Flammable refrigerant' warnings, or red markings on the tubing
Hissing, oily stains on tubing, or frost on a broken line

Gas, caravan, RV and silent minibar fridges with no compressor, and fridges from before about 1950: these may hold ammonia, sulphur dioxide or methyl chloride, which are poisonous, so keep their tubing sealed
do: Keep the sealed system closed: take fans, motors, wiring, thermostats and panels without cutting tubing
Take the whole unit if you need the compressor; a working fridge is worth more whole
Treat flammable refrigerants like propane: no sparks or flames nearby
Ventilate well if a line breaks, and keep out of low spots where gas collects
dont: Don't cut, drill or unbraze tubing on a unit that still holds gas
Don't use a torch or grinder on refrigerant lines
Don't open a sealed system in a small room or basement
Don't attempt refrigerant recovery without training and a recovery machine
ppe: Thick gloves; liquid refrigerant causes frostbite

Work only in well-ventilated areas: refrigerant vapour is heavier than air, collects in low spots and can suffocate without warning. A leak detector only finds leaks; it can't tell you whether the air is safe
firstAid: Frostbite from spray: the Emergency Response Guidebook says only medical personnel should thaw it. With none to hand, and only if it can't refreeze, soak it in 37–39 °C water for about 30 minutes; don't rub. Blisters or numbness need medical care (see Cold)
Spray in an eye: rinse with lukewarm water for at least 15 minutes and get medical help

Dizziness or breathlessness after a leak: get to fresh air. Don't go down into a basement or pit after someone who collapsed until it's aired out, or you'll collapse too; collapse needs CPR and medical care
